title: The pocket trumpet from Bill Ratzenberger and sitting in with Clark Terry
summary: She talked a pocket trumpet out of a Connecticut music-store owner and surprised Clark Terry at a concert by joining the blues.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Cornet or trumpet: choosing and owning horns

So you were playing it
then, weren't you?

Yeah. Well I was just
going through the motions.
I'm still shy when it comes to just
standing up there taking -- I wouldn't think of taking

a solo. But if the guys are playing ensemble, I'd like to find a note and go along with them.
And I got a few bars going for me. I know what I'm doing but I'm just chicken, see.
So later on, I was -- I began to get a few gigs up in Fairfield, Connecticut at the Continental which is owned and operated by Bill Ratzenberger.
So one day, I had been cleaning out the horn and I forgot to take the spring out. And I sprained the spring in the instrument.
And Bill Ratzenberger happened to have a music store, and he manufactured a mouth piece called the 'jet tone mouth piece.' He was a very good musician. He plays the trumpet himself.
So I told him what had happened. So he said, 'Bring the horn up and I'll fix it for you.' So I took it up there and he put brand new springs in all my valves.
And what I would do as a surprise -- you know, at the end of the evening when I get through singing -- the band would start playing 'The Saints'?

and I'd come out from behind the curtain and start playing 'The Saints'. And this got to be a big thing.

And so one evening, I was up there and someone had brought him a small pocket trumpet from Germany. And he had it laying on the table where we were sitting, and I said, 'I've got to have one of those. I've got to have one.' I think it was my birthday, too.
So, by the end of the evening, I had talked him out this pocket trumpet. So now I've got that instrument.
And I am --
You played it in public?
Yeah, I play it quite often now.
I mean, I take it around with me and --
You do?
Oh yeah, I take it on the job. If there's a group there that's got a horn, I'll play it. I don't like to play it if there's just a trio there, because they'll expect me to play it all

night.
But if there's a band there or even
one other instrument, I'll probably go out just for
fun.

I've played along with some of the
greats. In fact, when Bill first gave me the horn,
I was booked to appear on a concert in which Clark
Terry was on along with other guys.

And Bill had just given me the horn
about a week before. And he was at the concert and
he was anxious to see the expression on Clark
Terry's face when I turn around with this horn.

So, he said, "Come on, you got to do
it now."

So I went up to Hank, who was at the
piano.-- I had my back to Clark and --
Hank Jones?
Hank Jones, yes.

And we ran over the blues, you know,
in B-flat. So we rehearsed a little bit there right
there on stage.
And so when the band started playing the

blues, I turned around and I started playing along with them. And Clark Terry looked around and he cracked up when he saw me with that little pocket trumpet.
So I talked him out of a lot of valve oil that night, which he was very happy to give me.
But now, if I go on a job to sing, everybody will say, 'Did you bring your axe?' I'll say, 'Oh yeah!'
So I'll break out now with a few bars especially if they're going to play the blues. I got that down pretty pat now. I can improvise on the blues.
But I keep telling everybody I'm going really learn a complete solo. It may be 'Do You Know What It Means To Miss New Orleans'. Again, I know it already! All I got to do is practice it for this horn.
But one of my problems is, that I just don't get enough chance to practice these days, and don't get enough time to really sit down and woodshed.
